strengths: The problem is well motivated: exploiting known objective decompositions could improve distributional optimization in large discrete spaces.
Combining a tree-factorized search distribution with local value-weighted updates is a useful algorithmic direction, with connections to graphical models and policy optimization.

Experiments show substantial improvements over the naive EDA on several objectives, with 20 random seeds, separate hyperparameter tuning for both methods, and additional sample-budget and decomposition-threshold studies.
weaknesses: The central equivalence in Eq. 5 is false: summing subtree Q-functions double-counts downstream contributions and can change the optimizer. For binary root r and child c, let f(r,c)=3(1-r)+r(2-c). Then Q_root=3-r and Q_child=r(2-c). The original objective is maximized at r=0 with value 3, whereas Q_root+Q_child is maximized at (r,c)=(1,0), where f=2. Consequently, Eq. 6 and the subsequent lower-bound derivation do not establish optimization of the stated objective. This is a fundamental technical flaw, even if the implemented updates have empirical utility.

The update derivation has additional unresolved issues. In Eqs. 34–35, the conditional target's normalizer generally depends on the parent assignment and cannot be pulled outside the parent expectation as a single constant. Also, targets proportional to Q times the current distribution require nonnegative weights, which the unrestricted objectives do not guarantee. Exponential shaping ensures positivity in experiments but does not validate the unshaped derivation.

Algorithm 1 does not clearly implement the conditional expectations in Eq. 7. Line 9 uses an unnormalized sum, reuses the sample index, and does not specify how descendants are sampled conditional on each fixed parent assignment. Pooling descendants from different parent contexts would not generally yield an unbiased conditional estimate. This ambiguity affects both correctness and sample-cost accounting.

The only experimental baseline is a decomposition-unaware EDA. Search-distribution architecture and weighting strategy change simultaneously, so the experiments cannot isolate the benefit of message passing. Comparisons with FDA and an otherwise identical tree-factorized EDA using global weights are particularly important given the novelty claims.

The synthetic evaluation uses only one randomly generated objective per sequence length and singleton-node trees. Twenty optimization seeds do not establish robustness across objective instances or junction-tree structures. These objectives also permit inexpensive exact dynamic programming, yet optimality gaps are not reported. There are no wall-clock, memory, or comprehensive component-evaluation comparisons to substantiate computational efficiency.

The protein experiments evaluate generated sequences using the same fitted predictor being optimized. They demonstrate surrogate optimization, not validated improvements in scientific design. The manuscript acknowledges predictor error as outside scope, but its practical-utility claims remain stronger than the evidence, especially for unrestricted optimization beyond predominantly single- and double-mutant training data.

strengths: The problem is relevant: exploiting known objective decompositions could improve distributional optimization in large discrete spaces. Combining factorized search distributions with local value functions is a useful direction.
The experiments show substantial improvements over the chosen naive EDA on several synthetic and protein-derived objectives, particularly in optimization speed.
Separate hyperparameter tuning for both methods, 20 optimization seeds, sample-budget experiments, and the decomposition-threshold case study provide useful empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The central derivation contains a false objective equivalence. Equation 5 claims that maximizing f is equivalent to maximizing the sum of subtree Q-functions, which double-counts descendant contributions. Consider a binary root r and child c, root rewards [10, 0], zero child rewards, and edge rewards [[1, 0], [7, 0]]. The original objective is maximized at (r,c)=(0,0), with value 11. However, Q_root=[11,7], and Q_root+Q_child is maximized at (1,0), with value 14 versus 12. Consequently, Equations 6–11 do not establish the claimed optimization equivalence. This does not prove the implemented heuristic cannot work, but it invalidates its principal theoretical justification.

Additional derivation errors are substantive. In Equation 35, the conditional target's normalizer generally depends on the parent assignment and cannot be removed as a single global constant. Appendix A.4 also defines V=log sum exp(Q), whereas the claimed normalized distribution exp((Q−V)/beta) requires V=beta log sum exp(Q/beta). Furthermore, the fixed-sample term −beta log p in Equation 51 does not represent the entropy objective in Equation 50. The alternative derivation therefore does not repair the main argument.

The Monte Carlo message estimator is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1, line 9, uses an unnormalized sum and reuses the sample index inside and outside that sum. More fundamentally, Equation 7 requires child samples conditional on a particular parent assignment; pooling children from joint samples with different parents does not estimate this conditional expectation. The manuscript needs an unambiguous estimator and its sampling cost before the implementation can be assessed reliably.

The sole experimental baseline changes both the search-distribution factorization and the weighting rule. Consequently, the results cannot isolate the contribution of message passing. A baseline using the same junction-tree factorization with global objective weights is particularly important. The closely related FDA discussed in Section 3 is not evaluated, and classical exact message passing is omitted even on the tractable synthetic trees.

The efficiency and generality claims exceed the evaluation. Synthetic experiments use one sampled objective per reported length and singleton-node trees; repeated optimizer seeds do not measure variation across landscapes. There are no wall-clock, memory, or comprehensive component-evaluation comparisons, and no systematic scaling study with clique or separator size. Equal numbers of complete samples do not by themselves establish equal computational budgets.

The protein experiments establish optimization of fitted surrogate functions, rather than independently validated design improvements. The paper explicitly excludes predictor unreliability, which is a legitimate scope choice, but its practical scientific-design claims should remain correspondingly limited. Predictive validation is not reported comprehensively across the datasets, and accuracy near predominantly low-order mutants does not establish accuracy on optimized sequences.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: exploiting known objective decompositions to improve distributional optimization over large discrete spaces. Combining factorized search distributions with local value-based updates is a promising direction.

The reported results show substantial improvements over the selected autoregressive EDA baseline on several synthetic and protein-derived objectives. Experiments include 20 optimization seeds, separate hyperparameter tuning for both methods, and sample-budget ablations.

The contact-threshold study usefully explores the tradeoff between predictive accuracy and decomposability. The manuscript also acknowledges cases where the methods perform similarly and limitations of structure-derived decompositions.
weaknesses: The central derivation contains an invalid equivalence. Equation 5 replaces the original objective with a sum of subtree Q-functions, double-counting downstream contributions and potentially changing the maximizer. For a two-node tree, let root rewards be (10, 0), child rewards zero, and edge rewards have rows (0, -1) and (6, 5). The original objective prefers root state 0, achieving 10 rather than 6; the summed Q-objective prefers root state 1, achieving 12 rather than 10. Thus Equations 5–6 and the subsequent lower-bound argument do not establish the claimed optimization equivalence. The update may admit another justification, but the presented theoretical foundation requires substantial correction.

Additional derivation and algorithm details remain problematic. In Equations 34–35, the conditional target's normalizer generally depends on the parent assignment and cannot simply be removed from the outer expectation for shared neural parameters. Algorithm 1, line 9, uses an unnormalized sum with a reused sample index and does not specify how samples drawn under different parent assignments estimate the required conditional expectation. These issues make the implemented estimator and its relationship to the theory unclear.

The comparison does not isolate the proposed message-passing contribution: DADO changes both the search-distribution factorization and the update weights relative to the sole baseline. A matched factorized EDA using global weights is essential. The closely related Factorized Distribution Algorithm is discussed but not evaluated, leaving the incremental benefit over existing decomposition-aware approaches unresolved.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Results primarily measure progress per iteration at equal full-sequence sample counts, without wall-clock comparisons or accounting for conditional sampling and component evaluations. The synthetic objectives have single-variable tree nodes, permitting inexpensive exact dynamic programming, yet neither exact optimum gaps nor comparisons with that reference are reported. Moreover, optimization seeds are repeated on only one landscape per sequence length, limiting evidence across problem instances.

The protein experiments establish optimization of fitted surrogates, rather than improved scientific designs: the same predictor supplies both the optimization target and evaluation score. Predictor reliability on the generated sequences is not independently assessed, and predictive accuracy is not systematically reported across datasets. Although the paper explicitly sets model misspecification aside, this limits the practical significance supported by these experiments.

The novelty positioning is incomplete. The relationship to policy-gradient reward-to-go estimators and structured credit assignment needs sharper treatment; the broad claim that relevant policy optimization is restricted to chain graphs is insufficiently supported. Together with the theoretical errors and missing matched baselines, this prevents the promising empirical results from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The problem is well motivated: exploiting known objective decompositions could improve discrete distributional optimization. Combining factorized search distributions with local value functions is a useful direction.

The FDA baseline shares DADO’s search-distribution architecture, providing a meaningful comparison for isolating the contribution of local weighting. Experiments include extensive hyperparameter sweeps and 20 optimization seeds.

The appendix provides useful additional evidence, including seven protein-derived objectives, decomposition perturbations, predictive-accuracy comparisons, and runtime measurements. It also reports cases where FDA matches or exceeds DADO.
weaknesses: The central equivalence in Eq. 3 is false: summing subtree Q-functions double-counts downstream contributions and can change the maximizer. For a two-node binary tree, let the root contribution be h(0)=0, h(1)=3, the child contribution be zero, and the edge values be g(0,0)=2, g(0,1)=1, g(1,0)=g(1,1)=0. The original objective h+g is maximized at root=1 with value 3. However, Q_root=h+max_child g and Q_child=g, so their sum is maximized at (0,0), with value 4 versus 3 at root=1. Thus Eq. 4 and the subsequent lower-bound argument do not establish optimization of the stated objective. This is a fundamental flaw in the principal derivation, even if the eventual update could admit a different justification.

The conditional KL derivation in Appendix A.4.2 has another substantive error. The normalization of p*_n(child|parent) depends on the parent assignment, so Eq. 26 cannot extract a single constant Z outside the parent expectation. Removing this normalization changes the weighting of parent contexts for a neural conditional model. Moreover, validity of a lower bound alone does not establish that maximizing it improves the original objective.

Algorithm 1 does not specify a valid estimator of its conditional expectations. Line 9 sums over K samples without normalization and reuses the outer sample index inside that sum. Samples from one joint batch do not generally provide K child samples conditional on each fixed parent assignment. Consequently, the implemented message estimator, its claimed unbiasedness, and its actual sampling cost cannot be established from the pseudocode.

The alternative maximum-entropy derivation does not resolve the soundness concerns. Equation 36 defines V=log(sum exp Q), but the claimed normalized conditional exp((Q−V)/β) requires V=β log(sum exp(Q/β)). The transition to Eq. 42 also replaces the entropy objective with a sampled negative log-likelihood term without accounting for the sampling distribution’s parameter dependence. These are mathematical discrepancies, not simply missing convergence guarantees.

The synthetic evaluation samples only one objective per principal sequence length and restricts nodes to single variables. Repeating optimization seeds does not establish robustness across landscapes or larger junction-tree cliques. These tree objectives also permit tractable exact optimization, yet the paper does not report optimality gaps or compare against exact message passing. The statistical-efficiency claim lacks a quantitative analysis or a systematic sample-budget study.

The scientific-design evidence establishes improvement of fitted surrogate scores, not improvement of independently assessed designs. The main text emphasizes four datasets selected partly for favorable decomposability, while the appendix shows weaker benefits relative to FDA for larger cliques. Predictive robustness under graph perturbations is useful but does not demonstrate optimization robustness under decomposition misspecification. These limitations substantially narrow the practical claims.

strengths: The problem is relevant: exploiting known objective decompositions could improve sample efficiency in discrete distributional optimization. Combining factorized search distributions with local credit assignment is a useful direction.

The experiments include EDA, FDA, and PPO baselines, method-specific hyperparameter searches, and 20 optimization seeds. FDA uses the same factorization and architecture as DADO, providing a meaningful comparison for the contribution of local weighting.

The appendix provides substantial additional evidence, including seven protein datasets, decomposition perturbations, larger synthetic problems, and runtime measurements. Reporting cases where FDA remains competitive helps characterize the method’s limitations.
weaknesses: The central objective equivalence in Eq. 3 is false: summing subtree Q-functions double-counts downstream contributions and can change the maximizer. For a root with states A/B, let its node reward be 3/0 and its child’s edge rewards be (0,0)/(2,0), with zero child node reward. The original objective prefers A, with value 3 versus 2, whereas Q_root + Q_child prefers B, with value 4 versus 3. This also invalidates the subsequent equivalence in Eq. 4. The final update may admit another justification, but the presented derivation does not establish it.

The conditional KL derivation has another substantive gap. In Eqs. 25–26, normalizing Q_i(x_i,x_parent) p_old(x_i|x_parent) generally requires a parent-dependent Z(x_parent), which cannot simply be removed from an expectation over parents when parameters are shared across parent contexts. Furthermore, optimizing the stated lower bound does not by itself establish improvement of the original objective.

Algorithm 1 does not clearly specify a valid Monte Carlo estimator of the conditional messages. Line 9 reuses the sample index and sums K child values without a 1/K normalization. Joint samples also do not automatically provide K conditional child samples for every fixed parent assignment. These ambiguities directly affect the claimed unbiasedness, computational cost, and reproducibility.

The synthetic evaluation uses only one randomly generated objective per main sequence length, so 20 optimization seeds do not establish robustness across landscapes or graph structures. These singleton-node tree problems also permit efficient exact max-sum optimization, yet no optimality gaps or exact-solver reference results are reported. This leaves the absolute quality of the solutions unclear.

The practical evidence establishes optimization of deliberately decomposed learned predictors, rather than improvement in independently assessed design quality. The paper explicitly defers predictor error, which is reasonable for an optimization study, but limits its scientific-design conclusions. Predictive robustness to graph perturbations does not establish that optimized candidates remain reliable outside the observed data distribution.

The main-text protein results emphasize four datasets with small junction-tree nodes. Appendix A.9.3 reports that DADO does not outperform FDA on GB1 and ynzC, indicating that the benefit depends materially on decomposition complexity. A systematic analysis across node size, overlap, and graph topology is needed to substantiate the broad efficiency claims.

The PPO comparison is limited: with one gradient step per fresh batch, the initial likelihood ratio is one, so clipping ordinarily does not constrain that update. This is weak evidence against a fully exercised PPO baseline. More broadly, the relationship to standard policy-gradient credit assignment needs sharper positioning, and the claimed statistical-efficiency advantage lacks a variance analysis.

strengths: The problem is relevant: exploiting known objective decompositions could substantially improve discrete distributional optimization. Combining factorized search distributions with subtree-specific credit assignment is a promising approach.

Experiments report consistent improvements on the main synthetic and four selected protein-predictor tasks, with 20 optimization seeds and method-specific hyperparameter searches. The FDA baseline shares DADO’s factorization, providing a useful control for the contribution beyond factorization alone.
The appendix provides substantial implementation details, additional datasets, runtime measurements, and investigations of predictive accuracy under changes to the decomposition graph.
weaknesses: The central objective equivalence in Eq. 3 is false: summing subtree Q-functions double-counts downstream contributions and can change the maximizer. For a binary root r and child c, let the root contribution be a(0)=0, a(1)=3, the edge contribution be b(0,c)=2-c, b(1,c)=-c, and the child contribution be zero. The original objective is maximized at (1,0), scoring 3. However, Q_r=max_c b+a and Q_c=b, so their sum is maximized at (0,0), scoring 4 versus 3 at (1,0). This also invalidates Eq. 4 and the corresponding appendix argument. The proposed updates might admit a different justification, but the supplied derivation does not establish them.

Further derivation issues remain. In Eqs. 25–26, the normalization of the conditional target generally depends on the parent assignment, so it cannot be removed as a single global constant outside the parent expectation. Moreover, maximizing the lower bound in Eq. 5 does not by itself establish improvement of the original objective. These gaps require a corrected analysis, rather than additional intuition.

The message estimator is not reproducibly specified. Algorithm 1, line 9, reuses the sample index inside an unnormalized sum over K joint samples. As written, this does not estimate the required conditional expectation for each fixed parent assignment. The paper needs to distinguish conditional resampling from a single sampled subtree return and explain the actual estimator used.

The synthetic evaluation uses only one random landscape per configuration; repeated optimization seeds do not establish robustness across landscapes. These singleton-node trees also permit inexpensive exact dynamic programming, yet optimality gaps are not reported. The PPO comparison is limited because only one gradient step is taken per sampling iteration, leaving its clipping mechanism largely untested.

The practical evidence establishes optimization of fitted surrogates, not improved real properties. This is consistent with the stated scope, but limits scientific-design claims. The main text emphasizes four favorable decompositions; Appendix A.9.3 acknowledges that DADO does not outperform FDA on GB1 and ynzC. Robustness studies primarily measure predictive accuracy, rather than downstream optimization robustness.

Several presentation choices obscure the magnitude and generality of the gains. The main protein plots use a data-dependent negative-log transformation that magnifies near-maximum differences, while original-scale results are relegated to the appendix. Quantitative effect sizes, diversity measurements, and performance versus treewidth would better support the claimed distributional and scalability benefits.
